content:
The short answer

If you only watch one, make it Klaus (2019), Netflix's hand-drawn Santa origin story and still the best Christmas film the service has made. For a big family night, The Christmas Chronicles (2018) puts Kurt Russell in the sleigh. For a musical, Jingle Jangle (2020). Everything below is on Netflix US at the time of writing, checked in November 2026. Netflix originals do not rotate out, and we have built most of this list from them; the two licensed favourites at the end are the ones to catch before they move. For the same films ranked against every other service, see our guide to the best Christmas movies of all time.

Christmas movies on Netflix at a glance

Streaming details are for the US and were checked in November 2026. Holiday catalogues shuffle a lot in December, so a quick search in the app is worth it before you promise anyone a specific film.

Film | Year | Director | Best for
Klaus | 2019 | Sergio Pablos | The one to start with
The Christmas Chronicles | 2018 | Clay Kaytis | Big family night
Jingle Jangle: A Christmas Journey | 2020 | David E. Talbert | A proper musical
That Christmas | 2024 | Simon Otto | Young kids
A Boy Called Christmas | 2021 | Gil Kenan | A gentle adventure
Falling for Christmas | 2022 | Janeen Damian | Rom-com night
Love Hard | 2021 | Hernán Jiménez | Rom-com with jokes
Love Actually | 2003 | Richard Curtis | Licensed — catch it now

For the whole family

These are the films that survive the hardest test in home cinema: grandparents, teenagers and a seven-year-old on the same sofa, all still watching at the halfway mark.

Klaus (2019)

A spoiled postal student, Jesper, is exiled to a frozen island town where nobody sends letters, and strikes a deal with a reclusive toymaker who carves toys he never gives away. Sergio Pablos, a Disney and Illumination veteran, made it with hand-drawn animation lit like a painting, and it gets more beautiful as it goes. It is an origin story for Santa that earns its ending without a single cheap shortcut. If your family watches one film from this list, this is the one — and because it is a Netflix original, it is not going anywhere.

The Christmas Chronicles (2018)

Two kids stow away in Santa's sleigh on Christmas Eve, crash it in Chicago, and have to help him save the night. The draw is Kurt Russell, who plays Santa as a charming, slightly roguish blues fan and clearly has the time of his life. There is a jailhouse musical number that should not work and completely does. A sequel followed in 2020, also on Netflix, and the pair make an easy double bill for Christmas Eve itself.

That Christmas (2024)

Richard Curtis wrote this animated anthology set in a snowy Suffolk seaside town, where a blizzard scrambles everyone's plans: a school play, a turkey shortage, a Santa stuck in the storm. It is built from Curtis's own children's books, and it has his usual mix of warmth and one joke aimed over the kids' heads every few minutes. At 91 minutes it is the right length for younger children, and the storm plot gives it more momentum than most gentle Christmas fare.

A Boy Called Christmas (2021)

A young boy named Nikolas travels into the far north looking for his father and a village of elves, with a talking mouse and a reindeer called Blitzen for company. It adapts Matt Haig's novel, keeps the book's bittersweet streak — this is a story about grief as much as magic — and casts Maggie Smith, Jim Broadbent and Kristen Wiig around its young lead. Best for children of seven and up who like their Christmas stories with a little sadness in them.

Jingle Jangle: A Christmas Journey (2020)

Forest Whitaker plays a legendary toymaker whose inventions were stolen by his apprentice; decades later his granddaughter turns up to put things right. David E. Talbert shoots it as a full stage musical that happens to be on film — big dance numbers, songs by John Legend's team, and sets you could get lost in. It runs just under two hours, so start it early with small children, but for a family that loves a musical there is nothing else on Netflix like it.

Rom-coms and cosy nights in

Netflix makes more Christmas rom-coms than anyone, and most are wallpaper. These four are the ones with actual jokes, chemistry or a hook worth the evening.

Falling for Christmas (2022)

Lindsay Lohan plays a spoiled hotel heiress who loses her memory in a skiing accident and is taken in by the widowed owner of a struggling lodge. You know every beat before it lands, and that is rather the point: it is Lohan's comeback film, she is good in it, and the whole thing is engineered to be watched under a blanket. The definition of a cosy night in.

Love Hard (2021)

A Los Angeles dating columnist flies to Lake Placid to surprise the man she matched with, and finds she has been catfished — then agrees to keep up the pretence for his family in exchange for a date with the real guy. Nina Dobrev and Jimmy O. Yang make a genuinely funny double act, and it is sharper about dating apps than most comedies that are actually about them. The best of Netflix's rom-com batch.

Single All the Way (2021)

Peter dreads going home to his family's matchmaking, so he brings his best friend Nick as a pretend boyfriend; his mother has already set him up with someone else. It was Netflix's first gay Christmas rom-com, with Jennifer Coolidge stealing every scene she walks into as an aunt with no filter. Sweet, well cast, and mercifully short on the genre's usual contrivances.

The Princess Switch (2018)

A Chicago baker and a European duchess who look identical swap lives for two days before Christmas. Vanessa Hudgens plays both, then comes back for two sequels as a third lookalike. It is nonsense, cheerfully, and it started Netflix's whole Christmas-universe habit. Watch it when you want the festive equivalent of a mug of hot chocolate: warm, sweet, gone in 100 minutes.

Hot Frosty (2024)

A widow puts a scarf on a snowman and he comes to life as a sweet, confused man who needs to learn about Christmas, radiators and personal space. Yes, really. Lacey Chabert and Dustin Milligan play it completely straight, which is why it works — it became a word-of-mouth hit in 2024 precisely because it commits to the bit. The silliest film on this list, and proud of it.

The licensed favourites — catch them while they're on

Most of Netflix's Christmas catalogue is its own, but a few studio films rotate through. These two were on Netflix US when we checked in November 2026; licensed titles are the ones that move, so watch them early in the season.

Love Actually (2003)

Richard Curtis's nine-stranded London rom-com is the most argued-about Christmas film ever made, and it is currently on Netflix US. Some stories have aged beautifully (Bill Nighy's washed-up rocker is still the funniest thing here), some less so, and the airport ending still lands. We place it lower only because it rotates off the service; our all-service best Christmas movies guide tracks where it lives each year.

Violent Night (2022)

David Harbour plays a burnt-out Santa who walks into a hostage situation at a rich family's compound and turns out to have a Viking past. It is bloody, funny and far better made than the premise suggests — think Die Hard played by a Santa who has genuinely had enough. Strictly for after the kids are asleep; our Christmas horror movies guide has more in this vein.

One for Christmas Eve, after bedtime

Carry-On (2024)

Taron Egerton is a TSA officer blackmailed into waving a dangerous bag through LAX security on the busiest day of the year, with Jason Bateman's voice in his earpiece. It is a lean, proper thriller that uses Christmas Eve as a pressure cooker rather than decoration, and it was one of Netflix's biggest films of the 2024 season. We rate it in our all-service Christmas list too; on Netflix alone, it is the grown-up pick.

We started with Netflix's own Christmas originals, because they stay on the service all year, then checked which licensed titles were on Netflix US in November 2026. Films had to earn a rewatch, not just a release slot: we cut perfectly pleasant rom-coms that blur together and kept the ones with a performance, a look or a joke you would remember in January. Availability changes, especially for licensed films, so everything here is phrased for the US catalogue at the time of writing.

content:
The short answer

Start with The Mitchells vs the Machines (2021): it is the rare family film that makes children laugh and parents feel something. For younger kids, Leo (2023) and Klaus (2019) are the safest bets on the service. Most of this list is Netflix originals, which stay put; the few licensed titles are flagged. Everything is on Netflix US at the time of writing, checked November 2026. If your kids are animation loyalists, our Toy Story 5 review covers the newest cinema trip. For December specifically, our Christmas movies on Netflix guide takes over from this one.

Family movies on Netflix at a glance

Ages are our guidance, not the official rating — every child is different, and we flag the films with sad or scary stretches so you can decide.

Film | Year | Best ages | Why it works
Leo | 2023 | 4–9 | A class pet's-eye view of growing up
Klaus | 2019 | 5+ | The beautiful one
KPop Demon Hunters | 2025 | 7+ | The phenomenon
The Sea Beast | 2022 | 7+ | A proper sea adventure
Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl | 2024 | 6+ | 70 minutes, all jokes
The Mitchells vs the Machines | 2021 | 8+ | The whole-family winner
Enola Holmes | 2020 | 11+ | A mystery with a heroine to root for
Family Switch | 2023 | 8+ | Body-swap chaos

For little kids (roughly 3 to 6)

Short attention spans, low tolerance for peril, high tolerance for songs. These three fit, and none of them will talk down to the adults in the room.

Leo (2023)

Leo is a 74-year-old lizard who has spent his life in a classroom terrarium, and when he starts talking to the students he decides to spend his last year fixing their problems. Adam Sandler voices him, gruff and warm, and the songs are better than they need to be. It is gentle about growing up, friendship and change, and at 102 minutes it just about holds a four-year-old. The class-pet framing gives it a structure little kids follow easily.

My Little Pony: A New Generation (2021)

Equestria has split into three tribes that no longer speak, and a young earth pony sets out to reunite them. It is bright, musical and built around kindness without being bland about it, and the 90-minute run flies by. Parents who grew up with the older series will find it a different, better-made thing. A good first 'proper film' for preschoolers who have outgrown episodes.

The Willoughbys (2020)

Four siblings with spectacularly selfish parents hatch a plan to send them on a dangerous holiday and become orphans on purpose. It is the darkest-humoured film in this section — think Roald Dahl by way of a Tim Burton storybook — so save it for five and six-year-olds with a taste for the macabre. Ricky Gervais narrates as a cat. The ending is genuinely sweet, which the film earns by being so cheerfully horrid first.

For ages 7 to 10

The golden zone: old enough for real adventure and a few scares, young enough that the whole family still watches together. Netflix is unusually strong here, in animation especially.

KPop Demon Hunters (2025)

A K-pop girl group who are secretly demon hunters, defending their fans from a rival boy band of actual demons. It became Netflix's most-watched film ever in 2025, and the songs are the reason your children already know it. The animation pops, the action is cartoonish rather than frightening, and the story about shame and friendship gives it a heart under the glitter. If your house has somehow missed it, start here.

The Sea Beast (2022)

In a world where sea monsters are hunted for sport, a young stowaway and a famous hunter end up on the wrong side of the story. Chris Williams, who co-directed Moana, makes it a proper swashbuckler — tall ships, storms, creatures the size of islands — with a brain: it asks who gets to write the history books. Karl Urban and Zaris-Angel Hator are excellent. One of the best-looking films Netflix has made.

Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl (2024)

Feathers McGraw, the silent penguin villain from The Wrong Trousers, returns after 30 years to take revenge via a fleet of robotic garden gnomes. Aardman's stop-motion is still made by hand in Bristol, and every frame shows it. At 70-odd minutes it is the shortest film on this list and the easiest sell for a mixed-age room: slapstick for the kids, film references and dry wit for the adults. A Christmas Day staple in Britain; a treat anywhere.

Finding 'Ohana (2021)

A brother and sister spending the summer in rural Hawaii find a journal pointing to a lost treasure, and set off with two new friends to find it. It has The Goonies' shape with a Hawaiian heart — the culture is the point, not the backdrop — and the adventure is pitched exactly right for this age group: caves, maps and mild peril. A live-action change of pace in an animation-heavy section.

We Can Be Heroes (2020)

When Earth's superheroes are captured, their children — parked in a government safe room — have to rescue them. Robert Rodriguez made it as a companion to The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl, and it has the same homemade energy: kids outsmarting every adult system in their way. It is aimed squarely at 7-to-10s rather than their parents, but it moves fast and its message about teamwork lands without a lecture.

For the whole family, grandparents included

The hardest slot to fill: a film a teenager, a parent and a grandparent will all still be thinking about at breakfast. These five manage it, with two honest parent notes along the way.

The Mitchells vs the Machines (2021)

A film-obsessed teenager's road trip to college collides with a robot uprising, and her technophobe dad becomes the only thing between humanity and the machines. From the team behind Spider-Verse, it looks like a scrapbook exploded — in a good way — and it is very, very funny. Underneath is the truest thing any family film has said about phones. Our number one pick for this list, full stop.

Guillermo del Toro's Pinocchio (2022)

Del Toro moves Collodi's tale to fascist Italy and makes it in stop-motion, and the result is the most beautiful film on this list and the saddest. This Pinocchio is about fathers, sons and death, and it does not soften any of it. We would save it for children of ten and up who can handle a film that will make the adults cry. It won the Oscar for animated feature, and it deserved to.

Enola Holmes (2020)

Sherlock's teenage sister, played by Millie Bobby Brown, out-detects both her brothers while searching for their missing mother. It is a romp with real momentum — chases, disguises, a suffragette plot underneath — and Enola's direct-to-camera asides make tweens feel like co-conspirators. Two sequels followed, the third in 2026, so a successful first watch buys you a whole trilogy. Best for 11 and up, though mystery-loving nine-year-olds will cope.

Family Switch (2023)

A rare astronomical alignment swaps a mum and dad with their teenage kids on the morning of the biggest day of each of their years. Jennifer Garner and Ed Helms lead a body-swap comedy in the Freaky Friday line, with the dog and the baby swapped for good measure. It will not change anyone's life, but it is warm, well-paced and lands its family-first ending. A safe Friday-night click.

Yes Day (2021)

For one day, two parents have to say yes to everything their three kids ask for, within a few ground rules. Jennifer Garner — who also produced it, from Amy Krouse Rosenthal's picture book — throws herself into water balloons, ice-cream challenges and a theme-park finale. It is slight, and it knows it, and most families will recognise the argument it is having about fun versus rules. Expect to be asked for a yes day afterwards.

Planning the holidays already? Disney Christmas movies covers the other big catalogue, our best Thanksgiving movies guide handles November, and our The Breadwinner review is worth a look if your family likes its comedy gentle.

Family films we have reviewed in full

Some of our favourite family films live in our review archive rather than on Netflix right now: the mouse-sized adventure of Stuart Little, the survival story of The Wild Robot, the imaginary-friend reunion in IF (2024), the true-story drama of The Blind Side, and the gentle octopus mystery of Remarkably Bright Creatures. Each review covers the story, the scares and the age guidance in full.

Planning December? Our guide to the best Christmas movies for kids sorts the season's family films by age, with honest notes on the scary and sad bits.

How we picked

We favoured Netflix originals, because licensed family films rotate off the service and a guide that points at missing films is no use to anyone. Within that, we picked for range: something for preschoolers, something for the 7-to-10 zone where Netflix is strongest, and films that hold a room of mixed ages. We have flagged the two that need a parent note — Pinocchio for its sadness, The Willoughbys for its gallows humour. Ages are our judgement; you know your children better than we do.

Karl Urban and Zaris-Angel Hator are excellent. One of the best-looking films Netflix has made.

Feathers McGraw, the silent penguin villain from The Wrong Trousers, returns after 30 years to take revenge via a fleet of robotic garden gnomes. Aardman's stop-motion is still made by hand in Bristol, and every frame shows it. At 70-odd minutes it is the shortest film on this list and the easiest sell for a mixed-age room: slapstick for the kids, film references and dry wit for the adults. A Christmas Day staple in Britain; a treat anywhere.

A brother and sister spending the summer in rural Hawaii find a journal pointing to a lost treasure, and set off with two new friends to find it. It has The Goonies' shape with a Hawaiian heart — the culture is the point, not the backdrop — and the adventure is pitched exactly right for this age group: caves, maps and mild peril. A live-action change of pace in an animation-heavy section.

When Earth's superheroes are captured, their children — parked in a government safe room — have to rescue them. Robert Rodriguez made it as a companion to The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl, and it has the same homemade energy: kids outsmarting every adult system in their way. It is aimed squarely at 7-to-10s rather than their parents, but it moves fast and its message about teamwork lands without a lecture.
For the whole family, grandparents included
The hardest slot to fill: a film a teenager, a parent and a grandparent will all still be thinking about at breakfast. These five manage it, with two honest parent notes along the way.

A film-obsessed teenager's road trip to college collides with a robot uprising, and her technophobe dad becomes the only thing between humanity and the machines. From the team behind Spider-Verse, it looks like a scrapbook exploded — in a good way — and it is very, very funny. Underneath is the truest thing any family film has said about phones. Our number one pick for this list, full stop.

Del Toro moves Collodi's tale to fascist Italy and makes it in stop-motion, and the result is the most beautiful film on this list and the saddest. This Pinocchio is about fathers, sons and death, and it does not soften any of it. We would save it for children of ten and up who can handle a film that will make the adults cry. It won the Oscar for animated feature, and it deserved to.

Sherlock's teenage sister, played by Millie Bobby Brown, out-detects both her brothers while searching for their missing mother. It is a romp with real momentum — chases, disguises, a suffragette plot underneath — and Enola's direct-to-camera asides make tweens feel like co-conspirators. Two sequels followed, the third in 2026, so a successful first watch buys you a whole trilogy. Best for 11 and up, though mystery-loving nine-year-olds will cope.

A rare astronomical alignment swaps a mum and dad with their teenage kids on the morning of the biggest day of each of their years. Jennifer Garner and Ed Helms lead a body-swap comedy in the Freaky Friday line, with the dog and the baby swapped for good measure. It will not change anyone's life, but it is warm, well-paced and lands its family-first ending. A safe Friday-night click.

For one day, two parents have to say yes to everything their three kids ask for, within a few ground rules. Jennifer Garner — who also produced it, from Amy Krouse Rosenthal's picture book — throws herself into water balloons, ice-cream challenges and a theme-park finale. It is slight, and it knows it, and most families will recognise the argument it is having about fun versus rules. Expect to be asked for a yes day afterwards.

content:
The short answer

Disney+ is where the big Christmas catalogue lives. Home Alone (1990) is the essential stream; The Santa Clause (1994) is the best of the Santa films; and for animation, Mickey's Christmas Carol (1983) does Dickens in 26 perfect minutes. Everything below is on Disney+ in the US at the time of writing, checked November 2026. For the same season on every service, see our guide to the best Christmas movies of all time, and for Netflix's side of the story, our Christmas movies on Netflix list.

Disney Christmas movies at a glance

Disney owns most of its Christmas catalogue outright, so these films stay put year after year — the list below should look the same next December. Details checked on Disney+ US in November 2026.

Film | Year | Director | Best for
Home Alone | 1990 | Chris Columbus | The essential
The Santa Clause | 1994 | John Pasquin | The Santa story
Mickey's Christmas Carol | 1983 | Burny Mattinson | The classic short
Mickey's Once Upon a Christmas | 1999 | Alex Mann et al. | Little kids
The Muppet Christmas Carol | 1992 | Brian Henson | The best Dickens
Noelle | 2019 | Marc Lawrence | A modern original
The Nightmare Before Christmas | 1993 | Henry Selick | Halloween or Christmas?
Disney's A Christmas Carol | 2009 | Robert Zemeckis | The faithful one

The animated classics

Disney was making Christmas cartoons before most studios existed, and the short films are where the catalogue is strongest. They are also the part of the catalogue that changes least: these shorts have been December fixtures for decades, passed from one generation's television schedule to the next generation's streaming queue. Three of these run under half an hour, which makes them perfect early-December viewing.

Mickey's Christmas Carol (1983)

Scrooge McDuck was born to play Ebenezer Scrooge — the character was named for him — and this 26-minute featurette casts Mickey as Bob Cratchit, Goofy as Jacob Marley and Jiminy Cricket as the Ghost of Christmas Past. It retells Dickens faithfully, jokes and all, at a pace modern family films could learn from. It was Disney's first Mickey theatrical short in 30 years, and it still feels like the definitive cartoon Christmas Carol.

Mickey's Once Upon a Christmas (1999)

Three stories in one: Donald's nephews wish for Christmas every day and learn why that is a curse, Goofy tries to prove Santa is real to a doubting Max, and Mickey and Minnie each secretly sell what they love most to buy the other's present. Made direct-to-video in 1999, it has become the default first Christmas film for a generation of children. Gentle, funny, and done in just over an hour. A computer-animated second volume followed in 2004; the hand-drawn original is the one to watch.

Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas (1997)

Set inside the first film's timeline, while Belle is still a prisoner: she stages a Christmas against the Beast's orders, and a pipe-organ villain (Tim Curry, having a wonderful time) schemes to keep them apart. The original cast returned, the songs are better than a direct-to-video sequel deserves, and it gives the enchanted-objects cast a whole film to shine. A curiosity that turned into a tradition in a lot of houses. It also answers a question the original film left open: what Christmas looked like in that castle in the last year before the rose's final petal fell.

Olaf's Frozen Adventure (2017) and Prep & Landing (2009)

Two shorts worth pairing. Olaf's Frozen Adventure sends Frozen's snowman door to door collecting other families' traditions, and its 22 minutes are a good test of whether your household is ready for more Frozen. Prep & Landing is the cleverer piece: a crack team of elves who prepare houses for Santa's arrival, played like a spy film. Both are on Disney+, and together they fill exactly one cosy half-hour.

Live-action family favourites

The films Disney+ subscribers actually open every December. Between them they cover slapstick, Santa lore and the best screen Scrooge of all.

Home Alone (1990)

Eight-year-old Kevin McCallister is left behind when his family flies to Paris, and defends the house from two burglars with paint cans, tarantulas and total conviction. Chris Columbus directs, John Williams scores, and Macaulay Culkin gives one of the great child performances — the slapstick is famous, but the film works because Kevin's loneliness is real. All six Home Alone films are on Disney+; the first two are the ones that matter, and this is the one that matters most.

The Santa Clause (1994)

Tim Allen plays a toy-company executive who startles Santa off his roof on Christmas Eve and, by putting on the suit, legally becomes Santa — the 'clause' of the title. The transformation effects still hold up, the North Pole workshop is a delight, and the custody subplot gives it more heart than the premise promises. Both sequels and the follow-up series, The Santa Clauses, are on Disney+ too, so the whole run is in one place.

The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992)

Michael Caine plays Scrooge dead straight while surrounded by felt, which is both the joke and the reason this might be the best Dickens adaptation ever filmed. Gonzo narrates as Dickens himself, Kermit is Cratchit, and the songs are by Paul Williams. We rank it in our all-service best Christmas movies guide as well; on Disney+ alone it is the grown-ups' pick of the family shelf.

Noelle (2019)

Anna Kendrick plays Santa's daughter, who has to find her brother (Bill Hader) when he gets cold feet about inheriting the job days before Christmas. It was one of Disney+'s launch originals in 2019 and it has settled into the catalogue nicely: Kendrick is charming, the Phoenix-set fish-out-of-water middle is funny, and it treats the 'who is Santa now?' question with more care than most. The modern original to try once the classics are done.

Dashing Through the Snow (2023)

A social worker who hates Christmas (Chris 'Ludacris' Bridges) takes his daughter on a Christmas Eve call-out and meets a man in a red suit (Lil Rel Howery) who insists he is the real thing. It is a Disney+ original with a warm centre and a nice line in scepticism — the film is on the daughter's side throughout. A newer, gentler option for families who have worn out the nineties favourites.

For grown-ups and franchise fans

Not everything in the Disney+ Christmas section wears a Santa hat. These three are for the older end of the sofa.

The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993)

Jack Skellington, king of Halloween Town, discovers Christmas Town and tries to take over the holiday, with Danny Elfman's songs carrying the whole beautiful stop-motion enterprise. Tim Burton's story, Henry Selick's direction — and the annual argument about whether it is a Halloween or a Christmas film is now part of the tradition. Our answer: it streams on Disney+, it opens at Halloween and ends at Christmas, and it works watched at either. See our Christmas horror movies list for its darker cousins.

Disney's A Christmas Carol (2009)

Robert Zemeckis's motion-capture version casts Jim Carrey as Scrooge and all three ghosts, and it is the most faithful mainstream adaptation: whole passages of Dickens's prose survive, and the Victorian London it builds is genuinely eerie. The ghosts here are frightening in a way the cartoon versions are not, so keep it for older children and adults. Underrated, and the closest the Disney catalogue gets to a ghost story.

The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special (2022)

A 44-minute Marvel special: Drax and Mantis fly to Earth to kidnap Kevin Bacon and give him to Peter Quill as a Christmas present. James Gunn writes it as a love letter to the terrible Star Wars Holiday Special of 1978, and it is funnier and sweeter than it has any right to be. For franchise families it is the easiest win in this section — one episode's length, no homework required.

Splitting your December between services? Our family movies on Netflix guide covers the year-round movie-night list, and Christmas movies streaming maps the whole season across Netflix, Disney+, Hulu and Prime Video.

Choosing for a particular age? Our guide to the best Christmas movies for kids sorts Disney's Christmas films alongside every other service's, with the scary bits flagged.

How we picked

Disney's Christmas catalogue is mostly films Disney owns outright, so unlike the rotating licensed titles elsewhere, these stay on Disney+ all year — we checked the US service in November 2026 and weighted the list toward the films families actually rewatch: the two 1990s giants, the cartoon shorts that predate most of their audience, and the handful of Disney+ originals that have earned a place beside them. If a film is here, it is because we would put it on again this December.

content:
The short answer

Hallmark's Countdown to Christmas 2026 is the biggest the event has ever been: 34 new movies across ten weekends, from October 16 to December 20. If you only watch five of the new ones, make them Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story, The Nights Before Christmas, Double Booked for the Holidays, Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True and A Grand Biltmore Christmas. If you are here for the classics, start with Three Wise Men and a Baby and A Biltmore Christmas. Every premiere streams on Hallmark+ the day after it airs — and as we explain below, Hallmark+ is now effectively the only streaming home these films have.

Countdown to Christmas 2026 at a glance

Premiere dates are Hallmark Channel (US), 8 p.m. ET/PT unless noted. Every film below streams on Hallmark+ the next day.

Film | Premiere | Stars | Why watch
Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story | Oct 17 | Lyndsy Fonseca, Robert Buckley | The year's NFL film — a reporter profiles a Bears superfan
What If Christmas | Oct 25 | Lori Loughlin, Tom Cavanagh | An alternate-reality drama with real emotional stakes
The Nights Before Christmas | Nov 14 | Tyler Hynes, Laci J Mailey | A Christmas Eve time loop from a Hallmark fan favourite
Mistletoe and Mimosas | Nov 15 | Tamera Mowry-Housley, Kristoffer Polaha | Rival bar owners battle through a 12 Days of Christmas contest
Double Booked for the Holidays | Nov 22 | Rachael Leigh Cook, Owain Yeoman | Twins running a Welsh bookshop meet another set of twins
Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True | Nov 28 | Lacey Chabert, Christy Carlson Romano | A family Christmas filmed in the Disney parks
A Grand Biltmore Christmas | Dec 5 | To be confirmed | The follow-up to the 2023 hit A Biltmore Christmas
Save the Date for Christmas | Dec 20 | To be confirmed | The final premiere of the season

The 2026 premieres to prioritise

Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story (October 17)

The headline premiere of opening weekend. Reporter Avery (Lyndsy Fonseca) returns to Chicago to profile a beloved Bears superfan and enlists his firefighter grandson Matt (Robert Buckley). It is the third film in Hallmark's NFL partnership, after the Chiefs and Bills editions — and those two were among the most-watched premieres of their years, which tells you the formula works: football for the sceptics, romance for everyone else.

What If Christmas (October 25)

The season's most ambitious premise. Erin (Lori Loughlin), a heart surgeon's wife who feels her life has no purpose, receives a heart-shaped ornament and wakes in an alternate reality where her choices went the other way. Tom Cavanagh co-stars. Hallmark does one of these Sliding Doors dramas most years, and this is the one people will still be discussing in January.

The Nights Before Christmas (November 14)

Tyler Hynes is the closest thing Hallmark has to a leading-man brand, and this is his 2026 vehicle: Marty wishes for more time and wakes to Christmas Eve on repeat, falling for journalist Chloe (Laci J Mailey), who forgets him every loop. Time-loop romances live or die on the lead's charm offensive — Hynes has carried weaker premises than this.

Mistletoe and Mimosas (November 15)

Consultant Claire (Tamera Mowry-Housley) inherits her uncle's Christmas-themed bar — and its debt — and ends up in a 12 Days of Christmas contest against the bar owner next door (Kristoffer Polaha). A competition structure gives this one more plot than most, and Polaha is quietly one of the network's best actors.

Double Booked for the Holidays (November 22)

The season's most charming setup: identical twins Abigail and Charlie spend a week running a bookshop in Wales and meet another set of twins. Rachael Leigh Cook leads, the Welsh setting is a genuine change of scenery for Hallmark, and the twin mechanics give the script two romances for the price of one.

Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True (November 28)

The event premiere of Thanksgiving weekend. Lacey Chabert — Hallmark's defining Christmas star — plays Lindsey, whose family Christmas at Walt Disney World goes sideways when her room turns out to be next door to a man from a disastrous first date (with Christy Carlson Romano along for the chaos). A Hallmark movie actually set in the Disney parks is a licensing crossover that would have been unthinkable a few years ago.

A Grand Biltmore Christmas (December 5)

A follow-up to A Biltmore Christmas (2023), one of the most acclaimed Hallmark films ever made, returning to the Biltmore Estate with new characters, Elizabeth and Michael. Sequels to beloved Hallmark titles are rare enough to be news on their own; if it captures half the original's time-slip romance, it will be the December premiere everyone talks about.

More premieres worth your weekends

The rest of the schedule, by weekend. Opening weeks: 'Tis the Season for Setups (Oct 16, a party planner clashes with a ski instructor), Mr. & Mrs. Christmas (Oct 18, a town Christmas Market revival), Winter Wonderlanes (Oct 23, a bowling-alley rescue), Forgotten Holiday (Oct 24 — the boldest premise of the year: a proposal, a crash, a boyfriend whose memory of the relationship is gone, and Janel Parrish retracing the romance to restore it), Who's Coming for Christmas? (Oct 30) and Adopting St. Nick (Oct 31).

November: A Danish Christmas (Nov 1, a family inn and a mistaken-identity travel writer), Holiday Unplugged (Nov 7, Nikki DeLoach dating again), A Season of Promises (Nov 8, estranged sisters), My Christmas Cowboy (Nov 13, Amy Acker and Luke Macfarlane). Thanksgiving week adds early-evening double features: Christmas Delivered (Nov 26), The Christmas Eve Feast and Return to Santa (Nov 27), The Most Wonderful Secret (Nov 28), Eight Nights for Love and Miles to Christmas (Nov 29). December: The Snowflake Effect (Dec 4), An Angel in My Stocking (Dec 6), Christmas in Canterbury (Dec 11), Snow Globe Town (Dec 12), Noelle Nomads (Dec 13), Hearts All Aglow (Dec 18), Barking All the Way (Dec 19) and the season finale, Save the Date for Christmas (Dec 20).

The classics fans rewatch every year

Three Wise Men and a Baby (2022)

Three brothers (Tyler Hynes, Andrew Walker, Paul Campbell) are left caring for a baby over Christmas, and the network's three biggest male stars turn it into the defining Hallmark film of the decade. It now has two sequels — Three Wiser Men and a Boy (2024) and Three Wisest Men (2025) — and Hallmark+ carries extended cuts you cannot see anywhere else. Watch all three in order.

A Biltmore Christmas (2023)

A screenwriter (Bethany Joy Lenz) is sent back to the 1947 set of a classic Christmas film at the Biltmore Estate and falls for its leading man (Kristoffer Polaha). Regularly ranked the best Hallmark holiday movie ever made, and the reason the December follow-up above exists.

Christmas Under Wraps (2014)

A doctor (Candace Cameron Bure) takes a job in a remote Alaskan town and finds more than she bargained for. Long cited as Hallmark's highest-rated premiere, and still the template the network's Christmas films are measured against.

The Nine Lives of Christmas (2014)

A firefighter (Brandon Routh) adopts a stray cat and meets a veterinary student (Kimberley Sustad). The cat-matchmaking plot sounds like a joke until you watch it — this is the connoisseur's pick, the one fans name when they say Hallmark films are better than their reputation.

Crown for Christmas (2015)

content:
The short answer

Hulu is the Christmas service people forget to check, and in 2026 that is a mistake. On November 20 it added a batch of genuine classics — National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, A Christmas Story, The Polar Express, Four Christmases, Fred Claus and Jack Frost — on top of its own originals (Happiest Season, The 12 Dates of Christmas, Nutcrackers) and a grown-up shelf that includes Die Hard, The Holiday and The Family Stone. If you already pay for Hulu, you may not need another service this December. Everything below was checked on Hulu US on November 23, 2026.

Christmas movies on Hulu at a glance

Streaming details are for the US, checked November 23, 2026. Titles marked 'Dec 1' arrive with Hulu's December batch.

Film | Year | Best for | Note
National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation | 1989 | Comedy night | Arrived Nov 20; on Hulu through year-end
A Christmas Story | 1983 | Families, nostalgia | Arrived Nov 20
The Polar Express | 2004 | Young kids | Also on HBO Max
Happiest Season | 2020 | Rom-com with depth | Hulu Original — never rotates off
The Holiday | 2006 | Rom-com night | Cameron Diaz, Kate Winslet
Last Christmas | 2019 | Rom-com/drama | Emilia Clarke, Henry Golding
The 12 Dates of Christmas | 2026 | New-release fans | Hulu Original, premiered Nov 6
Die Hard | 1988 | The annual argument | Die Hard 2 is on Hulu too
The Family Stone | 2005 | Family drama | Funny, then quietly devastating
Jingle All the Way | 1996 | Family comedy | Schwarzenegger hunts the sold-out toy
Miracle on 34th Street | 1994 | Gentle classic | The 1947 original arrives Dec 1

The classics

National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation (1989)

The best Christmas comedy ever made, and the centrepiece of Hulu's November 20 batch. Clark Griswold's pursuit of the perfect family Christmas destroys his house, his tree and his sanity in ascending order. It is on Hulu through the end of the year — watch it in December, because January is too late for this one.

A Christmas Story (1983)

Ralphie wants a Red Ryder BB gun; every adult in Ohio tells him he'll shoot his eye out. The most quotable Christmas film ever made arrived on Hulu the same day as Christmas Vacation, which makes Hulu the rare service holding both halves of the American Christmas canon.

The Polar Express (2004)

Tom Hanks voices half the cast of Robert Zemeckis' motion-capture train ride to the North Pole. It is the definitive Christmas Eve film for younger children — gentle, musical and just eerie enough around the edges to feel magical. Also on HBO Max if your household splits subscriptions.

Miracle on 34th Street (1994)

The Richard Attenborough remake is on Hulu now, and the beloved 1947 original — Edmund Gwenn's Oscar-winning Kris Kringle — joins it on December 1. Watch the remake with the kids, then the original after they're in bed, and decide the family argument properly.

Hulu originals and rom-coms

Happiest Season (2020)

Hulu's flagship Christmas original: Kristen Stewart and Mackenzie Davis as a couple going home for Christmas, where one family doesn't know they're a couple. Clea DuVall directs a rom-com that is genuinely funny and genuinely about something — the rare streaming-original Christmas film that will outlive its release year. As an original, it never rotates off the service.

The 12 Dates of Christmas (2026)

This year's new Hulu Original rom-com, premiered November 6: Lucy Hale and Ian Harding — a Pretty Little Liars reunion — in a dating-through-December story built for exactly the audience that will find it. If you watch one new TV-movie-style premiere this season that isn't Hallmark, make it this one. (For the full Hallmark slate, see our Hallmark Christmas movies guide.)

The Holiday (2006) and Last Christmas (2019)

The two rom-coms that anchor Hulu's December. The Holiday is the house-swap comfort film — Cameron Diaz and Kate Winslet trading homes and love lives — and Last Christmas pairs Emilia Clarke and Henry Golding with a George Michael soundtrack and a twist that recontextualises the whole film. Add Four Christmases (2008), which arrived November 20, for the broader Vince Vaughn/Reese Witherspoon version of the same evening.

For families

Jingle All the Way (1996) is Schwarzenegger as a desperate dad hunting the season's sold-out toy on Christmas Eve — broad, loud and perfect for kids aged seven and up. Fred Claus (2007), another November 20 arrival, gives Vince Vaughn the role of Santa's bitter older brother, with Paul Giamatti as Santa himself. Jack Frost (1998) — Michael Keaton returns as a snowman to the son he left behind — is the one to handle with care: it is a family film about grief, lovely but sad, and worth a warning for children who have lost a parent. Nutcrackers (2024), a Hulu Original directed by David Gordon Green, has Ben Stiller reluctantly raising his four nephews in rural Ohio; it is the most critically respected family film on this page.

For the youngest viewers, Hulu carries the Rankin/Bass specials that raised several generations: Frosty the Snowman (1969), Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970) and The Little Drummer Boy (1968) — 25-to-50-minute classics that work as a toddler's entire movie night. Our best Christmas movies for kids guide sorts all of these by age, with notes on the scary and sad bits.

For grown-ups

Die Hard (1988) and Die Hard 2 (1990) are both here, so the annual 'is it a Christmas movie' debate can be settled with evidence. The Family Stone (2005) starts as a meet-the-family comedy and turns, honestly, into the saddest film on this page — Diane Keaton anchors it. A Bad Moms Christmas (2017) (arrived November 1) is the R-rated option. Almost Christmas (2016) and The Family Man (2000) cover the warm family-drama slot, Why Him? (2016) the Christmas-set cringe comedy, and Christmas Eve in Miller's Point (2024) the indie corner — a shaggy, affectionate portrait of one family's Christmas Eve on Long Island.

Two holiday-adjacent dramas round out the shelf: Edward Scissorhands (1990), Tim Burton's snow-globe fable, and Little Women (2019), whose Christmas scenes carry the whole film. And for viewers who like their Dickens dark, FX's A Christmas Carol (2019) — Guy Pearce as a genuinely damaged Scrooge — is the anti-comfort version, streaming in full on Hulu.

Coming to Hulu on December 1

Hulu's December batch is family-heavy: Home Alone 2: Lost in New York plus Home Alone 3, 4, The Holiday Heist and Home Sweet Home Alone (the original stays Disney+ only); The Santa Clause 2 and 3 (the original, again, is Disney+'s); the 1947 Miracle on 34th Street; Ernest Saves Christmas (1988); The Preacher's Wife (1996) with Denzel Washington and Whitney Houston; While You Were Sleeping (1995); I'll Be Home for Christmas (1998); and Snow Dogs (2002). If your December watchlist leans family, Hulu on December 1 becomes a genuinely complete Christmas service.

Two originals worth a closer look

Nutcrackers (2024)

Ben Stiller's first leading role in years is a Hulu Original that deserves better than its quiet release: a workaholic Chicagoan inherits his sister's four unruly sons and the Ohio farm they refuse to leave. David Gordon Green directs it loose and warm, and it is the rare modern family film that trusts silence and weather. It sits in our families section above, but it plays just as well for adults — think of it as the Hulu Christmas film for people who do not usually watch Hulu Christmas films.

Christmas Eve in Miller's Point (2024)

The indie pick. One extended Italian-American family, one Long Island Christmas Eve, shot like a memory — grain, glow and overlapping dialogue. Nothing much 'happens', which is the point: it is the most truthful film on this page about what a big family Christmas actually feels like at 11 p.m. Stream it after the relatives leave.

Already have Hulu through the Disney bundle?

A practical note that changes the maths: if your Hulu comes with the Disney bundle, Disney+ is effectively the same app shelf — which means the films Hulu lacks are one tile away. Home Alone, The Santa Clause, Noelle and The Muppet Christmas Carol all live on Disney+ (see our Disney Christmas movies guide), and between the two services a bundle household can watch nearly every major Christmas film except the Netflix originals. Hulu's own shelf above is what makes the combination complete.

content:
The short answer

Peacock should be the best horror service in America: it is NBCUniversal's own streamer, which makes it the natural home of Universal Pictures and Blumhouse — the two biggest horror catalogues there are. The reality is strong but patchier than the theory. The best horror movie on Peacock right now is Get Out (2017), and around it sit the Blumhouse Halloween films, M3GAN, Five Nights at Freddy's, a superb Hitchcock shelf and the complete Chucky TV series. But several famous Universal titles have rotated away (we list them honestly at the end), so this guide earns its keep. Everything below was checked on Peacock Premium US on November 23, 2026.

Horror on Peacock at a glance

Included with Peacock Premium (US), checked November 23, 2026.

Film | Year | Type | Note
Get Out | 2017 | Social thriller | The service's flagship horror film
Halloween | 2018 | Slasher | Legacy sequel to the 1978 original
Halloween Kills | 2021 | Slasher | The brutal middle chapter
M3GAN | 2023 | Tech horror | Theatrical and unrated cuts; 2.0 arrives Nov 26
Five Nights at Freddy's | 2023 | Supernatural | The animatronic hit — the teen gateway pick
Alien: Romulus | 2024 | Sci-fi horror | Arrived Nov 21 — the month's biggest addition
Psycho | 1960 | Classic | Hitchcock's blueprint for the slasher
Black Christmas | 1974 | Proto-slasher | The film that invented the genre's grammar
Shaun of the Dead | 2004 | Horror-comedy | The best rom-zom-com ever made
Freaky | 2020 | Slasher-comedy | Body-swap slasher with Vince Vaughn
Happy Death Day | 2017 | Time-loop slasher | Light, clever, endlessly rewatchable
Drop | 2025 | Thriller | A Peacock exclusive first-date nightmare

Modern essentials

Get Out (2017)

Jordan Peele's debut is the defining horror film of its decade — a weekend meeting the parents that tightens like a vice. It is Peacock's flagship for a reason, and if your subscription exists for one film, it is this one. Note that Peele's catalogue is split across services: Us is on HBO Max and Nope is on Netflix, so Peacock alone will not complete the trilogy.

Halloween (2018) and Halloween Kills (2021)

Blumhouse's legacy sequels bring Jamie Lee Curtis back as a Laurie Strode who has spent forty years preparing for Michael Myers. The 2018 film is the strongest Halloween sequel ever made; Kills is meaner and more brutal, a mob-violence parable with a body count. Watch them back to back — but know the trilogy's finale, Halloween Ends, sits on Netflix, and the 1978 original is on Shudder and AMC+ (see the honesty section below).

M3GAN (2023)

A lifelike doll built to protect a grieving girl takes her programming literally. Peacock carries both the theatrical and unrated cuts — watch the unrated one — and M3GAN 2.0 arrives as a Peacock exclusive on November 26. Killer-doll horror with a satirical streak about parenting by tablet.

Five Nights at Freddy's (2023)

A night security guard, a derelict pizzeria, and animatronics that move when unobserved. The games' enormous young audience made this one of the biggest horror hits of its year, and it is the most-requested title on this page for teenagers: genuinely creepy, light on gore.

Freaky (2020) and Happy Death Day (2017)

Christopher Landon's two slasher-comedies are Peacock's most rewatchable horror. Freaky swaps a serial killer (Vince Vaughn) into the body of a teenage girl; Happy Death Day loops a student through the day of her own murder until she solves it. Both are funnier than they need to be and scarier than they look.

Drop (2025) and The Woman in the Yard (2025)

The year's two Blumhouse originals. Drop — a Peacock exclusive — traps a widowed mother on a first date with a blackmailer messaging her phone. The Woman in the Yard is slower and sadder: Danielle Deadwyler, a grief-stricken mother, and a motionless veiled figure on the lawn. Watch Drop for tension, The Woman in the Yard for dread.

The classics shelf

Peacock's Hitchcock collection is a genuine asset: Psycho (1960), the blueprint every slasher since has copied; The Birds (1963), nature-attack horror before the genre had a name; and Vertigo (1958), the obsessive psychological thriller that regularly tops greatest-film polls. Add Black Christmas (1974) — Bob Clark's proto-slasher, which invented the call-is-coming-from-inside-the-house grammar four years before Halloween — and Peacock holds a short course in horror history that Netflix cannot match.

Horror-comedy and the Chucky universe

Shaun of the Dead (2004) remains the best horror-comedy ever made, full stop. Renfield (2023) gives Nicolas Cage a full Dracula turn in a gore-comedy about his servant's toxic workplace (watch it soon — it joins Netflix on December 9 and may rotate). And Peacock is the US home of Chucky: the three-season TV series streams only here, alongside the sequel run — Child's Play 2 and 3, Bride of Chucky, Seed, Curse and Cult. The 1988 original is the odd one out, sitting on MGM+ and AMC+.

New on Peacock in November 2026

November was a strong month: Alien: Romulus (November 21) is the headline — Fede Álvarez's back-to-basics Alien film is the best thing to happen to that franchise in decades. Never Let Go (November 19), a Peacock exclusive with Halle Berry protecting her sons from an evil only she can see, and the folk-horror You Won't Be Alone (November 16) and Firestarter (2022, November 12) round out the additions, with M3GAN 2.0 closing the month on November 26. On the TV side, all three seasons of Chucky and the Peacock originals Teacup and Hysteria! are here, and Crystal Lake — the Friday the 13th prequel series — has been streaming since October 15.

Not on Peacock — and where they actually are

The most useful paragraph in this guide, because 'Universal film' no longer means 'on Peacock': Us is on HBO Max. Nope, The Black Phone, Jaws and Halloween Ends are on Netflix. Halloween (1978) is on Shudder and AMC+. The Thing (1982), An American Werewolf in London and Candyman (2021) are on Prime Video. Wolf Man (2025) is on Hulu, Speak No Evil (2024) is on Starz, and Abigail (2024) currently has no US subscription home at all. Peacock's catalogue rotates monthly — Jaws, Him and The Invisible Man all left during 2026 — so treat any older guide (including, eventually, this one) with suspicion and check the app.

Horror TV: Peacock's secret weapon

Peacock's horror series bench is stronger than any rival's. Chucky (2021–24) is the headline: Don Mancini, the franchise's creator, ran all three seasons as direct continuations of the films, with Brad Dourif voicing Chucky throughout — and Peacock is its only US streaming home. Teacup (2024), produced by James Wan, is folk-horror about a Georgia family sealed inside an invisible boundary. Hysteria! (2024) plays the 1980s Satanic panic as horror-comedy. And Crystal Lake, the Friday the 13th prequel series, premiered on October 15 and is still the service's most talked-about horror title this autumn.

What to watch tonight, by mood

With teenagers: Five Nights at Freddy's, then Freaky — creepy premises, comedy release valves, no nightmares that outlast the weekend. On a date: Get Out if you want to talk afterwards; Shaun of the Dead if you do not. When you cannot sleep afterwards anyway: Black Christmas (1974) followed by Psycho — seventy years of slasher history in one double bill, and still the two most unsettling films here. A weekend binge: Halloween (2018) and Halloween Kills on Peacock, then cross to Netflix for Halloween Ends — annoying that the trilogy is split, but the films themselves are worth the app-switch.

How we picked

Every title was checked against Peacock Premium's US catalogue on November 23, 2026, using JustWatch US and Peacock's own listings; November additions come from Peacock's announced schedule. We ranked on quality first and Peacock-exclusivity second — a great film you can only see here outranks a great film that is everywhere. Peacock Premium costs $12.99 a month in the US (Premium Plus, ad-free, is $19.99); the cheaper Select tier excludes the movie catalogue. author: Maryam Afaq

faqs.question: What is the best Christmas movie for toddlers?
faqs.answer: Angela's Christmas (2017) on Netflix — 30 minutes, gentle throughout, made for the youngest viewers. That Christmas (2024) and Frosty the Snowman (1969) on Hulu are the next step up.

faqs.question: Is Home Alone OK for a 5-year-old?
faqs.answer: We would wait. Home Alone is rated PG, and most of it is cartoon slapstick, but the burglars' injuries are played as real pain, Kevin's fear early on is genuine, and younger children often fixate on the 'left behind' premise. Most kids love it from seven or eight — it is perfect there.

faqs.question: Is The Nightmare Before Christmas too scary for kids?
faqs.answer: It depends on the child. It is spooky rather than gory — skeletons, ghouls and the burlap villain Oogie Boogie are the peak scares — and most children from seven handle it happily. Sensitive five- and six-year-olds may find Halloween Town intense; try Klaus first.

faqs.question: Where can we watch A Charlie Brown Christmas?
faqs.answer: On Apple TV+, which holds the Peanuts specials exclusively. It is not on Netflix, Disney+ or Hulu, which is why it is not in the main list — but at 25 minutes it remains the perfect Christmas Eve watch if you have the service.

faqs.question: What is the best Christmas movie for a mixed-age family?
faqs.answer: Elf (2003) on HBO Max or Prime Video — physical comedy for the little ones, quotable lines for the adults, nothing that will upset anyone. Klaus (2019) on Netflix is the other unanimous pick.

content:
The short answer

The best Christmas movie for your child depends on the child, so this guide is sorted by age rather than ranked. Toddlers: Angela's Christmas and That Christmas. Ages five to seven: Klaus, The Polar Express and The Muppet Christmas Carol. Ages eight and up: Home Alone, Elf and A Christmas Story. Under each film we note the bits that might scare or sadden — because every parent has been caught out by a 'family classic' with one scene too many. Streaming homes are US, checked in November 2026. For the grown-up ranking, see our best Christmas movies of all time.

At a glance: picks by age

Ages are our guidance, based on content rather than certificates alone. Runtimes help for school nights.

Toddlers and preschoolers (ages 2–4)

Angela's Christmas (2017, Netflix) is the gentlest Christmas film ever made: 30 minutes about a little girl in 1910s Ireland who takes the baby Jesus from the church crib to keep him warm. Nothing scary, nothing sad that isn't resolved, and short enough for the smallest attention spans. Frosty the Snowman (1969, Hulu) is the 25-minute Rankin/Bass special — a magician's hat, a melting that is undone within minutes, and songs toddlers can hold onto. That Christmas (2024, Netflix) adapts Richard Curtis's children's books into three linked stories; one involves a child briefly separated from parents in a snowstorm, handled warmly and quickly. The Grinch (2018, Peacock) is the softest Grinch: Illumination's version is bright, musical and entirely tantrum-free compared to the 2000 film below.

Ages 5–7: the sweet spot

Klaus (2019, Netflix) is the best film on this page: a selfish postman and a reclusive toymaker thaw a feuding town. One honest flag — the story's warmth is built on loss (a widower's grief, a town's feud), and sensitive six-year-olds may ask big questions afterwards. That is a feature, not a bug. The Polar Express (2004, HBO Max and Hulu) is the Christmas Eve ritual film; the ghostly hobo on the train roof is the one spooky beat. The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992, Disney+) is the finest Dickens adaptation for children, with one famous exception: the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come is genuinely eerie, and Michael Caine plays the scene straight. Preview those two minutes for sensitive viewers.

The Santa Clause (1994, Disney+) works from six — Tim Allen accidentally becomes Santa; the only wrinkle is a custody storyline younger kids will simply not register. Jingle Jangle (2020, Netflix) is a full musical with Forest Whitaker as a betrayed toymaker; at 119 minutes it is the long one in this band, so start it early. How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000, Peacock) is louder and stranger than the 2018 cartoon — Jim Carrey's Grinch delights most six-year-olds and overwhelms some.

Ages 7–10: bigger adventures

The Christmas Chronicles (2018, Netflix) puts Kurt Russell in the sleigh for a proper adventure — a crash-landing, a night in jail, an Elvis number — with mild peril throughout and a warm ending; seven is right. A Boy Called Christmas (2021, Netflix) is a British origin story for Father Christmas with real darkness in it (a cruel aunt, a troll, a parent's death in the backstory), which is exactly why eight-year-olds who find other Christmas films babyish love it. The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993, Disney+) is the spooky one: skeletons and ghouls, played as a musical. Oogie Boogie is the peak scare. Elf (2003, HBO Max and Prime Video) is the mixed-age group's unanimous film — a man-sized elf in New York, with jokes on two levels and nothing to upset anyone.

Jack Frost (1998, Hulu) needs the clearest warning in this guide: it is a lovely film about a father who dies and returns as a snowman to say goodbye properly. For most children it is moving; for a child who has lost a parent, choose the moment with care. Home Alone (1990, Disney+) belongs at eight-plus in our judgement (see the FAQs) — the trap sequence is cartoon violence played with real wincing, and the scary-neighbour subplot resolves into one of the great Christmas reconciliations. A Christmas Story (1983, HBO Max and Hulu) is the oldest-kid pick: 1940s nostalgia, mild language, a BB-gun morality tale, and humour pitched at children old enough to enjoy watching adults be ridiculous.

Short on time? Under 90 minutes

School-night and toddler-friendly runtimes: Frosty the Snowman (25 minutes), Angela's Christmas (30), The Nightmare Before Christmas (76), The Grinch (2018) and The Muppet Christmas Carol (85 each). A Charlie Brown Christmas (25 minutes, Apple TV+) is the other essential short — it streams only on Apple TV+, which is why it is not in the table.

Coming in December

Two dates for the diary: Diary of a Wimpy Kid Christmas: The Getaway arrives on Disney+ on December 4, and on December 1 Hulu adds Home Alone 2: Lost in New York and The Santa Clause 2 and 3 — so both big series can be completed across two subscriptions. Our Christmas movies on Hulu guide lists the full December batch.

The rest of the Rankin/Bass shelf

Hulu also holds the other two classic Rankin/Bass specials. Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970) — Fred Astaire narrating how Kris Kringle became Santa — is as gentle as Frosty and works for the same ages. The Little Drummer Boy (1968) needs one flag: beneath the famous song is a sad story involving loss and a fire, and it lands harder than its vintage animation suggests. Preview it for sensitive three-year-olds; by five, most children take it in stride.

The Christmas Eve question

What families actually put on, on the night itself, follows a pattern worth copying. For under-eights, The Polar Express is the ritual: train, hot chocolate song, Santa, bed — it ends at exactly the right emotional temperature. For a mixed-age room, The Muppet Christmas Carol holds everyone from five to ninety. And once the youngest is eight, Christmas Eve belongs to Home Alone, ideally with the sequel queued for Boxing Day (it joins Hulu on December 1, while the original stays on Disney+). One scheduling tip from experience: whatever you choose, start it earlier than feels necessary — no Christmas film survives contact with an overtired four-year-old at 9 p.m.

A note for babies' first Christmas

Honestly? The baby is choosing nothing — you are picking the film that will be playing in the photos. Put Angela's Christmas or Frosty on for the atmosphere, then watch Klaus for yourselves once they are asleep. The tradition can start properly next year.

How we picked

Films were chosen from our wider Christmas guides and re-sorted by the age they genuinely suit — which is not always their certificate. Age guidance weighs scariness, sadness, runtime and theme, and reflects the judgement we would apply to our own families; certificates are the official ratings (mostly PG, with The Muppet Christmas Carol and The Polar Express rated G). Streaming homes were checked in November 2026 against JustWatch US and each service's catalogue. For service-by-service lists, see our guides to Christmas movies on Netflix and Disney Christmas movies, and our family movies on Netflix picks for the rest of the year.

And once the youngest is eight, Christmas Eve belongs to Home Alone, ideally with the sequel queued for Boxing Day (it joins Hulu on December 1, while the original stays on Disney+). One scheduling tip from experience: whatever you choose, start it earlier than feels necessary — no Christmas film survives contact with an overtired four-year-old at 9 p.m.
A note for babies' first Christmas

Honestly? The baby is choosing nothing — you are picking the film that will be playing in the photos. Put Angela's Christmas or Frosty on for the atmosphere, then watch Klaus for yourselves once they are asleep. The tradition can start properly next year.
